title: Elizabeth Young wants the system that 'killed' her daughter fixed

By Sean Tarek Goodwin

Topic:Mental Health

Elizabeth Young's daughter Jade Young was killed in the Bondi Junction attack. (ABC News: Sarah Moss)

The mother of a Bondi Junction stabbing victim has joined with six mental health organisations to pressure the NSW government for a better response to the coronial inquest.

The state government on Wednesday said it supported 11 recommendations in full and two in principle.

Elizabeth Young said her daughter Jade died at the hands of Joel Cauchi in April 2024 "because our system failed".

Peak mental health groups and the mother of a Bondi Junction stabbing attack victim have warned the state government's response to the incident will not prevent similar tragedies.

The state announced this week it would accept the recommendations of the coronial report into the incident, but the groups say its full response tells another story.

The recommendations were the result of a five-week coronial inquest into the deaths of six people at Bondi Westfield in 2024, killed by Joel Cauchi during a psychotic episode.

The six people killed, clockwise from top left: Yixuan Cheng, Faraz Tahir, Jade Young, Pikria Darchia, Dawn Singleton and Ashlee Good. (Supplied)

The state this week said it supported 11 recommendations in full. Two others — for modelling of short-term accommodation in Greater Sydney for those experiencing mental health issues and homelessness and a review of NSW Ambulance's major incident response plan — were supported in principle.

The six groups, which represent mental health consumers, carers, and psychiatrists, said the government has declined to commit to concrete action and was withholding a key report into gaps in mental health funding.

The groups include BEING Mental Health, Mental Health Carers NSW, the Mental Health Coordinating Council and the Australian Society of Psychiatrists.

Elizabeth Young, whose daughter Jade Young was killed in the attack, said she was "cynical" about the government's response.

"Although I'm pleased that [the government] has addressed 11 of the 13 recommendations, I'm fairly sceptical about what will actually be done in the practical sense."

Australian Society of Psychiatrists chief executive Pramudie Gunaratne said the government's "in principle" commitments to key recommendations "kicks the can down the road".

"We've already seen how the years of inaction have resulted in a tragedy, and even after that tragedy, if nothing concrete happens … then it's a ticking time bomb waiting for another tragedy to occur," Dr Gunaratne said.

Pramudie Gunaratne said "concrete" action was needed. (ABC News)

She called on the government to act on recommendations to commit to fully funding supported housing for people experiencing mental health issues.

Giancarlo de Vera, the chief executive of BEING Mental Health, which represents people living with mental health issues in New South Wales, called on the government to do more.

"Goodwill is just a promise on paper; we really need commitments to address the structural issues that the coronial inquest found."

Opposition leader Kellie Sloane has called on the government to release the report into mental health funding gaps and address the "enormous strain" on the system.

"We are in a world of pain if this isn't addressed properly," Ms Sloane said.

"The state Labor government has a habit of commissioning reports and then not revealing the details.

"This is too important to hide away."

The NSW government has announced it will accept all recommendations directed towards it from the Westfield Bondi Junction coronial inquest, six months after the findings were handed down.

Minister for Mental Health Rose Jackson on Wednesday acknowledged the government needs to do more.

"We accept the principle that there does need to be more support for people who are living with complex mental illness to stay stable in their accommodation, but we're rolling out different programs in order to provide that," Ms Jackson said.

She said the government is planning to release the gap analysis into mental health funding and was working with the Mental Health Alliance to finalise it.
